Only enough to tell a floor-plan corpus from a CSV of house prices before
downloading either. Sizes are the hub's own and are not verified.

HubKind.description: Which mirror a row came from.

HubRow.description: One row of a hub dataset, as the hub sent it.

omitted.description:
Columns left out, and why they would have been.

Named, because a column that is simply absent reads as a column the
corpus does not have.

row.description:
Every column, under the corpus's own name for it.

Two substitutions, and both are about size rather than meaning: a cell
the hub sent as bytes becomes a path back into this process that
resolves them (see [`Hubs::cell`]), because a hundred rows of base64 is
a result heavier than the pictures it describes; and a cell too large
to carry is left out and named in [`omitted`](Self::omitted).

row_index.description:
Where it sat in the split. The only name a row has that the corpus did
not choose, and the one a family key is usually built from.

HubRowsPage.description: One page of a hub dataset's rows.

columns.description: What the corpus declares it holds. A script is written from this.

config.description:
Resolved, never echoed: what was actually read, which is what makes the
same call repeatable after a dataset gains a second split.

total_rows.description: The split's own count, when the hub reports one.

HubSearchPage.description: A page of results, and what each hub had to say about answering.

notice.description:
Repeated on every response rather than left to a tooltip, because it is
the one thing a reader of this list has to know about it.

HubStatus.description: Whether a hub answered, and if not, why.

error.description:
Present when the hub was asked and did not answer. A search with one
hub down is a partial answer, and saying which half is missing beats
both an error and a silently short list.

results.description: Rows this hub contributed to the page.

variable.description: What to set when `configured` is false.

HubsPage.description: What this instance can search, before anybody types a query.

notice.description:
The same sentence every search response carries. Repeated here so a
panel that renders the hub list before the first search has it.

HumanFinding.description:
A finding a person recorded.

Deliberately narrower than [`Finding`]: no byte offsets, because a reviewer
is describing a judgement rather than a match, and no `found_by`, because
the registry fills that in from the caller's identity. A client that could
name its own reviewer could file somebody else's approval.

block.description:
The authored block this step came from, for the canvas box that lights
up while it waits.

prompt.description: What is being asked, in the words the person reads.

role.description: The role that may answer. Checked when the answer arrives, never here.

expires_at.description:
When this identity stops being valid, as a Unix timestamp. `None` for
the anonymous identity, which never expires because it was never
issued.

groups.description:
What the provider asserted, verbatim. Kept beside the resolved roles so
an operator debugging "why is this person only a viewer" can see the
input to the mapping rather than guessing at it.

queues.description:
The worker queues this caller may claim attempts on.

Not a role, and it can only ever *narrow*: a token holds [`Role::Editor`]
whether or not it names a queue, and naming none is what every producer
token does. It is here rather than derived from the group mapping for
the same reason the role is — a queue is what a shared secret in a
worker's environment authorises, and a provider that grew a group
called `houses` must not thereby authorise claiming.

Empty on every human session on purpose. Claiming takes a lease that
something has to renew, and a browser is not that something.

roles.description: The roles the groups above resolved to, highest last.

subject.description:
The provider's stable identifier — `sub` on an OIDC token. Never the
email, which people change.

oneOf.description: The shapes of one revision — the accepted one, or the one asked for.

split.description:
Which side of the split this image's family is on, under the project's
current policy. Shown so a labeller knows whether they are drawing a
test case, which changes how carefully they draw it.

ImageDetail.description: Where one image's revisions and its head are read together.

ImageHead.description:
One image's mutable head: what it is, what has been drawn on it, and which
of those drawings is the truth.

accepted.description: The revision an export reads. Set only by acceptance.

group_id.description: The split key. Every rendering of one building shares it.

image_id.description:
SHA-256 of the bytes, lowercase hex. Computed by the server on upload
and never taken from the client.

level.description:
`ground_floor`, `attic`, `basement`. Free text, because the vocabulary
differs per supplier and guessing it wrong is worse than keeping theirs.

metadata.description:
Everything known about this plan that did not come from the pixels: the
room names and areas from the catalogue page, the plan's own dimensions,
the listing URL.

This is the field that makes OCR a cross-check rather than a source.

source.description: Where it came from — a supplier, a public corpus, a scan batch.

uri.description: Where the bytes are. `blob:<image_id>` for something uploaded here.

view.description:
What kind of picture this is, in the caller's own words.

Free text for the same reason `level` is: the vocabulary differs per
corpus, and an enum shipped here would be one project's list imposed on
every other. An export selects the views it wants by name, so a corpus
that mixes photographs with diagrams, or plans with elevations, keeps
the ones a model reads out of the ones it does not — by saying so
rather than by somebody remembering.

bytes_stored.description: Bytes stored. The number that answers "why is the bucket bigger".

fetched.description: Rows whose bytes this job downloaded and stored.

ImportJob.description: A resumable import, as it sits in the store.

cursor.description:
Pages already registered *and* whose result shard is stored. The resume
point.

pages.description: Pages this job will read, pinned when it was created.

reject_pages.description:
Pages that wrote a reject shard, so reading them is a seek rather than
a scan of every page of a million-row import.

rows.description:
Rows across those pages. The denominator a progress bar may use,
because it was counted rather than guessed.

shards.description:
One per finished page: what was registered, hashed. The version
material.

warnings.description:
Things that are not errors and that somebody has to read anyway.

Always present, even when empty: a client that has to distinguish
"no warnings" from "the field is missing" is a client with a bug
waiting in it.

ImportJobRequest.description: What a job was asked to do.

batch.description: The staged batch to read. Sealed by queueing, so its rows are pinned.

dry_run.description:
Check every row and register nothing.

It still downloads: a row with no content address is refused by the
registry, so a dry run that skipped the fetch would reject every row
and teach the reader nothing about the batch. Blobs are addressed by
their content, so a dry run followed by a real import stores each
picture once.

ImportManifest.description: What a finished import is, forever.

batch_digest.description:
The batch's own content address. Two manifests naming the same one read
the same rows.

fetched.description:
Rows whose bytes were downloaded from a hub and stored here.

Set by the caller that did the downloading, not by the import: this
module writes an object store and reaches nothing. Zero for a batch
whose pipeline had already stored its own bytes, which is every batch
that carries an `image_id`.

warnings.description:
Things that are not errors and that somebody has to read anyway.

Every one of these describes a state where the import succeeds and the
resulting corpus is quietly worth less than it looks.

dry_run.description:
Check everything and register nothing.

The default is false, but the panel always asks for a dry run first:
six hundred rows with a group key mapped from the filename is not
something anybody wants to discover after it is in the project.

evidence.description:
Who checked that assertion, where, and when. Recorded, never enforced —
see [`RightsEvidence`].

rights.description:
What the caller asserts may be done with every image in this batch.

One value for the batch rather than per row, because a licence is a
property of the corpus and a per-row field invites a pipeline to derive
it from a column — which is exactly the mirror's word, laundered
through a `withEntry`.

ImportRow.description:
One image a pipeline produced.

Deliberately the same field names as [`RegisterImageRequest`], minus what
the request supplies once for the whole batch. A Flow query that renames
its columns to these is the entire mapping layer.

group_id.description: The **building**, not the drawing. See the module docstring.

image_id.description:
SHA-256 of the bytes, when the pipeline has already fetched and stored
them. Absent for a row that only points at a remote file.

ImportSource.description: Where a batch came from, recorded on every image it produces.

claimed_license.description:
What the hub said the licence was. Kept verbatim and never believed —
it is evidence about the mirror, not about the data.

config.description:
The configuration and split the rows came from. `default`/`train` is
the common shape and not the only one, and a corpus whose `test` split
was imported as if it were `train` is a leak nothing downstream can
see.

curated_source.description:
The curated row this matched, if any. The presence of this is what lets
[`check_rights`] refuse an over-claim.

oneOf.description: The curated verdict, when there was one.

files.description:
The files this batch was read out of, with whatever digest the hub
stated for each.

The hub's word, kept as the hub's word — like `claimed_license`, and
unlike the per-image content address, which is computed here from bytes
this process hashed. Both are worth having: one says what the mirror
thinks it is serving, the other says what actually arrived.

hub.description:
`kaggle` or `huggingface`, or anything else for a pipeline that did not
start at a hub.

pipeline.description:
The Flow PHP that produced these rows. Provenance that survives the
import: "where did these six hundred images come from" has an answer
that is a script rather than a memory.

revision.description:
The commit the rows were read at.

A dataset id is a moving target: `main` is whatever the uploader
pushed last, so a corpus re-read a month later is a different corpus
under the same name — and a training run naming it is naming nothing
anybody can go back to. This is the field that makes "the images this
model learned from" a question with an answer.

Empty when the hub did not report one, which is recorded rather than
invented: a blank revision says the provenance is a name, and a made-up
one would say it is a commit.

events.description:
A batch. Publishing several events in one call is what keeps a chatty
producer from paying a round trip per token.

last_checkpoint.description:
The checkpoint of the last event written. A client can hand this to the
live stream to pick up exactly where its own write landed.

oneOf.description: An output of an earlier step, by name.
A value bound when the execution was requested.

InputBinding.description: Where one of a step's inputs comes from.

InputRequest.description: What a step is waiting for somebody to answer.

role.description: The role that may answer. Checked when the answer arrives.

Keypoint.description: One named position inside a keypoint instance.

visible.description:
False when the plan shows the element but not this position — a door
whose leaf is drawn open past the page edge still has a hinge.

color.description:
What the canvas draws it in. Presentation only; nothing downstream may
depend on it.

ignore.description:
Excluded from every training target and from the loss.

The furniture, the hatching and the title block are not background —
they are pixels a model must not be scored on either way. Marking them
is cheaper than labelling them and far cheaper than the false positives
they produce.

keypoints.description:
The named positions a [`GeometryKind::Keypoints`] class expects, in the
order the tool asks for them.

layer.description:
Which grid this class paints into when a revision is rasterised.

The generic form of a problem that does not look generic: some classes
*overlay* others and must not erase them. An opening in a wall, a
defect on a component, a marking on a road — in every case the thing
underneath is still there, and one grid could only represent the
overlay by deleting it.

So the schema says so. Classes on the same layer share one integer grid
and paint in declaration order, last wins; classes on different layers
never contend, and a model reads one head per layer. Most vocabularies
need exactly one layer and never set this.

links.description:
Named references this class may hold to other instances in the same
image: `wall` for an opening, `connects` for a door's two rooms.

name.description:
Stable machine name — `wall_exterior`, not `Exterior wall`. Renaming it
is a new schema version, never an edit.

optional_keypoints.description:
Keypoints that may be left out because the plan does not show them.
Everything else in `keypoints` is required.

LabelSchema.description:
The complete, versioned vocabulary of one project.

Content-addressed like everything else authored here: the version is the
digest of the classes, so an unchanged schema re-saved is the same version
and a renamed class is unmistakably a different one.

step.description: Per step — retrieval, embedding, rerank and the rest.

time_to_first_token.description: Time to first token, from the `gen_ai.first_token` span event.

LaunchAccepted.description: What came back. Not a result — nothing has finished.

reference.description: The engine's name for the execution it just created.

workflow_run_id.description:
Echoed back so the caller can subscribe to
`/api/v1/workflow-executions/{id}/stream` immediately — before the
producer has published anything, which is the interesting part of a
launch's first thirty seconds.

LaunchBody.description:
What a caller may ask to start.

Note what is not here, and it is the same absence as `RerunBody`: no
endpoint, no image, no command. `deny_unknown_fields` so an attempt to
supply one is a 400 rather than a field that is silently ignored and reads
as accepted.

inputs.description: Parameter name to value, bound to the types the engine declares.

workflow.description:
The engine reference from the catalog, e.g.
`lp:planner:production:house_dataset_curation:v7`.

workflow_run_id.description:
Supply one to join this execution to events a producer will publish
under an id it already knows. Left out, aiwatcher mints one and returns
it, which is what the panel follows.

LawfulBasis.description:
What makes keeping this lawful, in the producer's own words.

aiwatcher cannot check any of it and does not pretend to. What it can do is
refuse to hold content that never claimed one, and record the claim
verbatim so that an auditor asking "why was this row eligible" gets the
answer somebody actually gave rather than one reconstructed afterwards.

oneOf.description: It is this caller's, until [`DeciderLease::expires_at`].

Somebody else has it and it has not run out. Carries *when* it does, so
a second worker waits rather than polling — the one thing it can
usefully do with the refusal.

LeaseOutcome.description: What asking for a hosted run's decider lease did.

LeaseReleased.description: Whether the release found a lease this caller was holding.

LinkDef.description: One named reference from an instance to another instance.

min.description:
How many targets this link must have. `(1, 1)` for an opening's wall,
`(2, 2)` for the two spaces it connects.

targets.description: Classes the target may belong to. Empty means any class.

LiveEvent.description:
What a browser receives over SSE or WebSocket.

Kept small on purpose: the panel gets the event as it happened, not a
re-derived projection, and `checkpoint` is what a reconnecting client sends
back as `Last-Event-ID`.

workflow_id.description:
Carried for the same reason `conversation_id` is: the live channel is
filtered server-side, and a subscriber watching one workflow execution
cannot be served by resolving it to a set of run ids at subscribe time —
a stage that starts *after* the browser connected would be filtered out
by the set it was given.

oneOf.description: A replayed or live event.
The replay is finished; everything after this is live.

The requested cursor was too old to replay from memory and the log was
read instead. Surfaced so the panel can say so rather than pretend the
stream was continuous.

LiveFrame.description:
A frame in the live stream.

`Caught` is not decoration: it is what lets the panel switch from "loading
history" to "live" at the right moment, instead of guessing from a timeout.
It mirrors Emmett's `MessageSourceCaughtUp` control message.

redirect_url.description:
Where to send the browser to end the session at the provider too.
`None` when the provider declares no `end_session_endpoint`, in which
case clearing the cookie is all a sign-out can do.

block.description: The authored block this step came from, for the editor link.

code_revision.description:
`sha256` of the notebook source this plan pins. A managed run pins code
first; an editor test may use unsaved code and is marked ad hoc.

MessageId.description:
Unique id of a single event, used for deduplication.

Generated as a UUIDv7 when the producer does not supply one; ULIDs and any
other sortable opaque string are accepted on the wire.

MessageKind.description:
Emmett splits messages into commands and events; aiwatcher only ingests
events today, but the discriminator is on the wire from day one so adding
control commands later is not a breaking change.

MessageMetadata.description:
Everything about a message that is not what it says.

The four correlation ids are `aiwatcher-core`'s, unchanged: an execution's
`correlation_id` is normally its own id, and `causation_id` names the input
message that produced this output. A reactor's completion event is caused by
the command that dispatched it, which is what makes a stream readable as a
chain of causes rather than a list.

delta.description:
`current - baseline`, and `None` when either side is missing — a
missing metric is not a delta of zero.

runs_retained.description:
Runs the read model holds in total. A `runs_considered` well below this
means the filter is narrow; the two being equal *and* at the retention
cap means older runs have been evicted and the window is truncated.

ModelDetail.description:
One model, its head and one version's full record.

`head` is a field rather than a flattened one, unlike the annotation
registry's equivalent. Flattening reads better in the JSON and produces a
TypeScript intersection type that the panel then cannot narrow, so the
nesting is the price of the client being generated rather than written.

ModelHead.description:
One model's mutable head: its versions, newest first, and its labels.

Labels live here and nowhere else, exactly as a prompt's do: a version is
immutable and `production` is not.

labels.description: Label to version id. `production` is the one a deployment reads.

ModelMetrics.description:
What a version measured, split by which data measured it.

Two maps rather than one, because the distinction is the whole point.
`validation` is what the training loop watched and selected against;
`test` is what nothing was allowed to look at. A registry that merged them
would let a model be promoted on the number its own early stopping
maximised.

ModelPackage.description: Everything a serving runtime needs and is not allowed to guess.

artifacts.description: Every file, each with its digest. At least one.

dependencies.description:
Package name to version specifier. What has to be present for the
entry point to import.

entry_point.description:
What inside the package to load: a file name, a module path, a
`module:function`. Interpreted by the loader for that runtime and by
nothing else.

preprocessing.description:
What the trainer did to its inputs, in its own words: `resize:512`,
`normalize:imagenet`, `edge-grid:8`.

Free text and deliberately not executable. A package that shipped
preprocessing *code* would be a package that runs code in whatever
opens it, which is the thing [`Runtime::executes_packaged_code`] exists
to keep visible.

runtime_version.description:
The build of that runtime the artifact was written by: `2.4.1`,
`1.17`. An ONNX graph using an opset the server's runtime does not have
fails at load; saying which one it needs turns that into a deployment
decision rather than a crash loop.

checkpoint_uri.description: Where the weights are. A pointer, like every other artifact here.

oneOf.description:
What a serving runtime is handed, when the trainer declared one.

`None` for a version registered before packages existed, and for one
whose producer only had a checkpoint URI. A runtime that meets `None`
says so rather than guessing a loader — the same choice ADR_0019 makes
about a licence nobody recorded. See [`crate::package`].

reproducible.description:
False when the dataset is a mutable name rather than an immutable
export reference. Recorded rather than refused, and it is what blocks
a promotion.

version.description:
SHA-256 of what makes this version *this* version: the run, the
checkpoint, the dataset and the measurements. Registering the same
thing twice is one version.

ModelVersionSummary.description: A version as it appears in a list.

oneOf.description:
Which loader this needs, when the trainer said. On the summary rather
than only on the version so that "is there anything here a runtime
could serve" is a list read rather than a fan-out.

attempts.description:
How many times this node was started.

Counted by distinct span key, not by event, so a redelivery does not
invent a retry that never happened.

declared.description:
Whether the declared graph mentions this node.

`false` means something ran that the declaration does not know about,
which is a stale declaration and worth seeing rather than hiding.

publishers.description:
Who published this node's executions, from `data.published_by`.

Normally one entry, or none for a producer that does not say. **Two is
a finding**: exactly one party publishes a given attempt (ADR_0026), so
a node with both `engine` and a producer's own events is a managed step
whose producer code opened its own `node()` scope, and its attempt count
and duration are describing two things at once. The flag exists to make
that visible, not to resolve it — the resolution is in the producer.

run_id.description:
The run the node executed in. A stage-per-pod orchestrator gives every
node a different one; this is what links a node back to its trace.

NodeStatus.description:
Where one node of one execution got to.

Four states rather than three, and the extra one is the point: `Pending` is
a node the graph declares and nothing has started.

OptimizationOutcome.description:
What the registry decided about an optimisation.

Never taken from the client. An optimiser is the last thing that should
grade its own output: it selected the candidate by maximising the number it
is now reporting.

Two flat variants with the reason beside them rather than inside them, so
the JSON is `{"outcome":"rejected","reason":"variables_lost"}` and the
generated TypeScript is a string union. An enum carrying its payload would
serialise a level deeper and make every reader unwrap it.

OptimizationRecord.description:
One optimisation run against one prompt.

Written by whoever ran the optimiser — `deepeval`'s `PromptOptimizer` is
the case this was built for — and read by the panel as "what happened to
this prompt lately".

algorithm.description:
What produced the candidate, e.g. `deepeval/SIMBA`. Free text: the
registry does not have opinions about optimisers, only about evidence.

dataset.description:
Which cases each split was drawn from, ideally versioned. Two scores on
different cases are two facts, not a comparison — the same rule
`baseline_for` applies to evaluation reports.

dev.description: What the optimiser optimised against. Guides the search; proves nothing.

evaluation_id.description:
The evaluation report this optimisation published, where it published
one. The join between the registry and the log.

primary_metric.description:
The metric the verdict is decided on. Every other metric is reported
and none of them promotes anything — a gate with several thresholds is
a gate somebody will tune until it opens.

oneOf.description: Why it was rejected. Absent on an admission.

report.description:
Whatever the optimiser produced — `deepeval`'s serialised
`OptimizationReport`, an iteration trace, anything. Bounded by the
registry, not by this type.

test.description: The held-out split. The only evidence that admits a candidate.

variables_lost.description:
Variables the baseline declared and the candidate does not. Computed by
the registry from both texts.

OptimizationRequest.description: Record what an optimiser did to a prompt.

baseline.description:
The version it started from. Must already be in the registry: an
optimisation against a prompt nobody stored is a claim with no subject.

candidate_text.description:
The candidate's text. Published as a version as part of recording, so
the record cannot name a prompt that does not exist.

dev.description:
What the optimiser optimised against. Guides the search, proves
nothing.

evaluation_id.description: The evaluation report this run published, where it published one.

optimization_id.description:
The optimiser's own id where it has one — `deepeval` supplies
`OptimizationReport.optimization_id`. Derived from the request when
absent, so recording the same result twice writes one record.

primary_metric.description: The metric the verdict is decided on.

promote.description:
Move `production` to the candidate if — and only if — it is admitted.

Off by default. An admitted optimisation has cleared the evidence bar;
deploying it is still somebody's decision, and a registry that promotes
on its own makes every CI run a release.

test.description: The held-out split. The only evidence that admits a candidate.

OptimizationSummary.description: An optimisation without its report document.

Origin.description:
Who drew a shape.

The whole reason a model-assisted pass is affordable: pre-annotation is
welcome and is recorded as such, so an export can require that a human
looked at it. A field that defaulted to `human` for machine output would
make the distinction unrecoverable one import later.

OverlapPolicy.description: What to do when a slot comes round and the last one is still going.

ParameterKind.description: How a form should render one input.

PartSummary.description:
One part's shape, with none of its content.

What makes a tombstoned turn still legible: "an assistant message of three
parts, 4 kB of text and a tool call" is an auditable fact that survives the
erasure of the words.

PayloadPolicy.description:
Where a hosted execution's content lives.

The definition chooses, the deployment sets the default, and the free one is
the default: a hosted run starts with no archive, no key and no flag. There
is deliberately **no `plain`** — a plaintext payload in the object store is
readable by every process holding the bucket's credentials, which is
ADR_0021's argument for the key.

PayloadRef.description:
Where a hosted message's words are, and how big they were.

Never the words themselves. The digest is of the *plaintext*,
so a reader can tell whether what it fetched is what was appended — the
prompt registry's rule, in a fourth place.

reference.description:
Under `external`, a URI in the worker's own store — `agentic`'s SQLite,
MLflow, or `conversation://<turn>` when the agent already writes turns
to the archive. Under `sealed`, the archive key the crypt sealed it at.

digest.description: `sha256` of the plaintext, recomputed here rather than believed.

reference.description: What the workflow stream records, resolvable only through this instance.

id.description: Stable within one pipeline. What the edges name.

PipelineStage.description:
Which part of the feature/training/inference cycle a workflow belongs to.

A **hint**, and named as one everywhere it is rendered. It is derived from
the entity's own name and description, which is a guess: an orchestrator
has no field that says "this one produces datasets". The value is that a
picker in Data Curation can default to curation workflows instead of
listing every launch plan in the cluster; the cost of being wrong is a
filter somebody switches off, which is why nothing but presentation may
depend on it.

timeout_seconds.description:
Seconds. Per-runtime and explicit — never a global default, because the
number that is generous for a Flow query is a hang for a notebook.

PreferenceLabel.description: Which of two answers a reviewer preferred.

ProfileRecord.description: A profiler session, as the part somebody reads in a review.

summary.description:
Top operators, totals, memory peak — whatever the profiler bridge
produced. Free-form because the fields on a profiler event have moved
between framework releases more than once.

uri.description: Where the full trace is, for whoever wants to open it in a profiler UI.

ProgressRequest.description:
One batched write of progress.

Batched rather than four endpoints, because the client buffers: a six-hour
run should make one request per epoch, not four, and an epoch that is
retried after a network blip has to land on the epoch it already wrote
rather than beside it.

per_class.description:
Instances per class over accepted revisions only. The number that says
whether there are enough doors yet.

ProjectSummary.description: A project as it appears in a list, with the counts a reader wants first.

PromptDetail.description: One prompt, with enough to render its page in one request.

oneOf.description:
The version `production` points at, or the newest when no label has
been moved. Carried with its text so the page paints without a second
round trip — the text is the thing being looked at.

PromptHead.description:
A prompt's mutable head: the labels, the description, and the index of what
is stored under it.

**Derived, not authoritative.** The versions and the optimisation records
are the truth; this is what makes listing them one request instead of one
request per object. It can be rebuilt from the store at any time, which is
what makes a lost concurrent write survivable rather than a corruption.
The exception is [`Self::labels`], which exists nowhere else — a label is a
pointer somebody moved, not a fact about an object.

labels.description:
`production` → the version a deployment should read. Any other label a
team wants (`staging`, `canary`) works the same way.

PromptName.description:
A prompt's identity.

Deliberately without `/`. A name is a path segment in
`/api/v1/prompts/{name}/versions/{version_id}`, and a name that can contain
a separator makes that route ambiguous with every route below it. Namespace
with `-` or `.` instead: `planner.floor-plan.system`.

next_cursor.description: Pass as `after` for the next page. Absent on the last one.

total.description:
Prompts in the store, before the filter. The difference between this
and `prompts.len()` is what the filter removed.

PromptSummary.description: One row in the prompts list.

oneOf.description:
The most recent one, so the list answers "what happened to this prompt"
without a second request per row.

metadata.description: Anything the producer wants to carry: a git sha, a ticket, a locale.

model.description:
What it was written for. A prompt tuned on one model is not evidence
about another, and this is what says which.

notes.description: Why this version exists. The commit message of a prompt.

oneOf.description: The version this one was derived from, where there is one.

variables.description:
The `{{ placeholders }}` the text interpolates, sorted. Derived from
the text by [`variables_of`], never supplied — a declared list that
disagrees with the text is worse than no list.

PromptVersion.description: One immutable version of a prompt.

PromptVersionId.description:
`sha256(text)`, lowercase hex.

Content addressing is what makes publishing idempotent: a redelivered
publish, a CI job that runs twice, and a producer that hashes its own
prompt before sending it all land on one version.

PromptVersionSummary.description:
A version without its text.

The list view's row. Kept separate so listing a prompt with two hundred
versions does not transfer two hundred prompts.

Provenance.description:
Where this turn came from, in the telemetry that is still on the log.

Every field is a join back. The archive expires on its own clock, and when
it does these ids are what is left — which is the point of keeping them out
of the encrypted half. "This run used a model that answered badly" stays
answerable after the words are gone.

prompt.description:
The prompt version this turn ran on, where the producer knows it —
`planner.floor-plan.system@sha256`. The join ADR_0011 exists for.

ProvideInputBody.description: The answer a `HumanInput` step asked for.

attempt.description:
Which attempt asked. Named by the caller rather than read from the
step's latest: an answer typed against a question that has since been
retried is an answer to a question nobody is asking any more, and
silently applying it to the new attempt would record a human decision
that no human made.

response.description:
Whatever the question asked for, as JSON.

Any value, and deliberately not an object: a step that offered
`choices` is answered with one of them, which `decide` reads as a JSON
**string**. Declaring this an object made the contract unable to express
the commonest valid request, so the generated client could not send one.

PublicAuthConfig.description:
What the panel is told before anybody has signed in.

Public on purpose, and it is the only route reachable unauthenticated
besides the health probes: a panel that cannot ask "is there a login here,
and what is it called" has to guess, and guessing wrong means either a
sign-in screen on an instance with no provider or an endless 401 loop on
one that has.

enabled.description:
`false` when `AIWATCHER_AUTH_MODE=none`. The panel renders no sign-in
screen at all in that case.

issuer.description:
Shown in the panel's own diagnostics, so "which authentik is this
pointing at" is answerable without a shell on the pod.

login_url.description:
Where to send the browser to sign in. `None` in `proxy` mode, where
signing in is something that already happened before the request
arrived.

provider.description: What to put on the button — "authentik" by default.

PublishDatasetRequest.description: What one completed Flow execution contributes to the registry.

execution_id.description:
The managed execution that produced these rows, when one did.

Provenance and not identity, for `produced_by`'s reason and with a
second one of its own: the same rows published by a rerun are the same
version, and a version per run would be a version history about *when*.
What it buys is the join the other way — from a published dataset back
to the run, its waterfall, and its `step.*` on the event log. Absent for
a version the panel published from an ad-hoc query (ADR_0025 withdrew
that path for managed runs only).

pipeline.description: The exact script that produced `items`, even when it was not saved first.

produced_by.description:
The block chain that produced these rows, as `name@revision`.

Present when the execution came from the pipeline canvas rather than
from one script, and provenance rather than identity — like the recipe
name and the description, and for the same reason: a block dragged
across the canvas is a new pipeline revision and the same rows, and a
dataset version per canvas tidy-up would be a version history about
layout.

It matters because the Flow script alone does not describe this
execution: a notebook block ran between that script and these rows, and
the only place its settings and its pinned source are written down is
the pipeline revision this names.

recipe.description: Saved recipe name, when the run came from one.

produced_by.description:
`<pipeline name>@<revision>`, the authored revision — provenance, and
never part of a dataset version's identity.

PublishRequest.description: Publish a version, and optionally update the prompt around it.

description.description: Replaces the prompt's description when present.

label.description:
Move this label to the new version — `production` to make it live.

Optional, and separate from publishing, because storing a prompt and
deploying it are different decisions. A publish with no label is a
draft that everything can read and nothing is using.

notes.description: Why this version exists. The commit message of a prompt.

oneOf.description: The version this was edited from, where the caller knows.

tags.description: Replaces the prompt's tags when present.

created.description:
`false` when this exact text was already stored. Publishing is
content-addressed, so a re-run of the same job is not a new version —
and the caller usually wants to know which of the two happened.
False when this exact pipeline and exact ordered set of rows already existed.

queue.description: Which worker queue this is claimable on.

task_ref.description:
`name@version`: the registered name and the pinned code version a worker
must match before it may claim an attempt.

conversation_id.description:
The same `conversation_id` the telemetry carries. This is the join, and
a turn that invents one is a turn nothing can be traced back from.

message_id.description:
The producer's stable id for this message. Sending it twice replaces the
turn rather than adding one — a retried flush must not double a corpus.

occurred_at.description:
When the message was said, rather than when it arrived. Ordering within
a conversation uses arrival, because a producer's clock is not something
an export's determinism can depend on.

ordinal.description:
Position among siblings. Ties are broken by `message_id`, so a producer
that sends every turn at ordinal 0 still gets a deterministic order —
just not the one it meant.

policy.description:
Consent, retention and what the producer says it redacted. Required in
a protected deployment; recorded as `unknown` in an open one, which an
export then excludes by name.

turns.description:
One exchange, as a producer flushes it. Not a transaction — see
`Registry::record_batch`.

RecordedEvent.description: An event as a consumer sees it.

RecordedMessage.description: A message as the stream holds it.

RecordedMetadata.description:
What the store fills in. Emmett's `RecordedMessageMetadata`, plus the
aiwatcher-specific identity fields a projector would otherwise dig out of
`data` on every event.

span_key.description:
The key `span_id` derived from. Carried so a projector can group a
start and its end without re-deriving it.

created.description: False when this exact content was already stored under this turn id.

findings.description:
What the server's own scan found, whatever the producer claimed. Empty
is the common case and the one worth not celebrating: a clean scan is
the absence of a match, not evidence there is nothing to find.

RedactionRecord.description: What a producer says its own redaction hook did.

redactor.description:
The hook, versioned: `acme-scrubber@2.1`. A bare name is accepted and
is worth less — "which version of the scrubber ran" is the question
asked after something gets through.

replaced.description:
How many spans it replaced. Recorded rather than derived, because the
server sees only what is left.

rules.description:
The rule ids that fired. Empty is meaningful and common: the hook ran
and found nothing.

RegisterImageRequest.description: What is being asked for when an image is registered.

view.description:
What kind of picture this is, in the caller's own words.

Free text for the same reason `level` is: the vocabulary differs per
corpus, and an enum shipped here would be one project's list imposed on
every other. An export selects the views it wants by name, so a corpus
that mixes photographs with diagrams, or plans with elevations, keeps
the ones a model reads out of the ones it does not — by saying so
rather than by somebody remembering.

oneOf.description:
What a serving runtime will need. Optional, and validated when given:
a half-declared package is worse than none, because it reads as one.

run_id.description:
The run that produced it. Read for its dataset, framework and code, so
a version cannot claim provenance the run does not have.

created.description: False when this exact version already existed.

promotion_blocked.description:
Why a label cannot point here yet, if it cannot. Returned on the
*registration* so the answer arrives with the thing it is about, rather
than when somebody later tries to promote it.

total.description: Complete, even when [`rows`](Self::rows) is a page of a sample.

RejectReason.description:
Why a row did not become an image.

Coarser than the message, on purpose: a reason with a row count is what
somebody reads first, and "38 000 rows had no readable picture at the
address they named" points at a mapping mistake in a way that thirty-eight
thousand distinct sentences do not.

RejectedRow.description: One row that did not make it, kept whole.

detail.description: The sentence, verbatim. A count says how many; this says what to fix.

RerunAccepted.description:
What came back. Not a result — the work has not happened yet.

A rerun is accepted, not completed: the evidence that it ran is the events
it publishes, on the same log as everything else. `reference` is whatever
the orchestrator calls the thing it just queued, so a caller can find it in
that orchestrator's own console.

url.description: Where to watch it, if the orchestrator said.

RerunBody.description:
What a caller may ask for.

Note what is *not* here: an endpoint. The orchestrator to talk to comes
from this deployment's configuration, never from the request and never from
the log. aiwatcher runs inside the cluster, so a caller-supplied URL is a
request to reach the cluster's network on that caller's behalf.

from_node.description:
Resume from this node. Advisory — whether an orchestrator can start
mid-graph is its business, and aiwatcher cannot verify that it did.

workflow_run_id.description: The execution to repeat. Omit for a fresh run of the workflow.

RerunRequest.description:
What is asked of the orchestrator.

Deliberately thin, and deliberately not a description of *how* to run
anything: aiwatcher knows the shape of a graph because a producer declared
it, not because it can execute one. Everything here is a name the producer
already chose.

from_node.description:
Resume from this node rather than from the start.

Advisory: whether an orchestrator can resume mid-graph is its business,
and one that cannot is free to start over. aiwatcher cannot verify the
difference and does not claim to.

workflow_id.description: The orchestration to run. Always present.

workflow_run_id.description:
The execution being repeated, when there is one. `None` asks for a
fresh execution rather than a repeat of a particular traversal.

ResolvedWindow.description:
Exact bounds, in seconds since the epoch. A relative window resolved once,
at compile time, so that a retry three hours later reads the same rows.

ResourceRequest.description:
What a package needs in order to run at all.

Declared so a scheduler can refuse rather than thrash. A model that needs
24 GB of accelerator memory placed on a node with 16 does not fail at load
— it fails at the first request under load, at which point the previous
version is already gone.

gpus.description:
Accelerators, and how much memory each needs. `None` means it runs on a
CPU, which is a claim rather than a default: a package that needs one
and says nothing gets scheduled somewhere it cannot run.

RetentionPolicy.description:
How long the content may be held, on a clock of its own.

Deliberately unrelated to the event log's retention. The log holds
operational fields and is sized for a volume; this holds somebody's words
and is bounded by what they were told. Tying them together would mean
raising the log's retention silently extends a consent nobody re-asked for.

policy_id.description: Which written policy this is. Recorded, never interpreted.

RetryPolicy.description:
How many times, and how far apart.

The defaults are three attempts, 1 s / 5 s / 30 s. The delays
are a list rather than a base and a multiplier so that a policy can be read
off the plan without arithmetic, and so that a runtime whose useful backoff
is not exponential can say so.

# Two budgets, because there are two kinds of failure

`max_attempts` counts attempts that **produced an answer**: the code ran and
was wrong, the query would not parse, the graph does not bind. Three is
right for those, because the fourth will be just as wrong.

`max_unavailable_attempts` counts attempts where nobody answered — the
service was down, the connection reset, the caller stopped waiting. Those
say nothing about the work, and spending the work's budget on them means a
forty-second outage kills a run that would have succeeded a minute later.
Measured, not supposed: restarting the process with the query service down
burned all three attempts and failed a chain whose Flow step was fine.

The two are counted separately off the attempt records the state already
keeps, so a run alternating between the two kinds is bounded by both.

delays_seconds.description: Seconds before attempt 2, 3, … . The last entry repeats.

delays_seconds_unavailable.description:
The same, for an attempt nobody answered. Longer, because what it is
waiting for is a service coming back rather than a flake passing.

max_attempts.description: Attempts that got an answer and the answer was wrong.

max_unavailable_attempts.description: Attempts where the runtime never answered. Its own budget — see above.

ReviewRequest.description: A change to an image's review state.

revision.description:
Which revision is being accepted. Required for
[`ReviewState::Accepted`], refused otherwise — accepting "whatever is
newest" is the same mistake as launching without pinning a version.

ReviewState.description: Where a revision sits between drawn and trusted.

RevisionSummary.description: A revision as it appears in a list, without its shapes.

per_class.description:
Instances per class, which is what tells a reviewer at a glance that a
plan has nine rooms and no doors.

per_origin.description:
Instances per origin. A revision that is entirely `model` has not been
looked at, whatever its review state claims.

RightsEvidence.description:
Who checked a rights assertion, where, and when.

The missing half of [`UsageRights`]. That type records *what* somebody
claimed; this records the claim's provenance — and the two are separate
because a claim with nothing behind it is still the claim that was made,
and pretending otherwise would mean either refusing it (which teaches
people to invent a licence to get past the dialog) or believing it.

Every field is optional and the whole thing is recorded rather than
enforced. What it changes is what a later reader can do: "why is this
corpus marked commercial" has an answer that is a URL and a name and a
date, instead of a `git blame` on a JSON file. The one hard rule stays
where it was — [`check_rights`] refuses a claim the curated table
contradicts, because there a human already read the licence at the source.

[`primary_source_url`](Self::primary_source_url) is deliberately named for
the *original*, never the mirror. ADR_0019's whole finding is that a hub
restates licences wrongly often enough that its card is evidence about the
mirror rather than about the data, so evidence pointing back at the hub
result somebody clicked is not evidence at all.

primary_source_url.description:
Where the licence was read: the paper, the project page, the repository
the corpus was published from. Not the Hugging Face or Kaggle card.

reviewed_at.description: When they read it. A licence at a URL is a licence on a date.

reviewed_by.description: Who read it. A person, because a rights assertion is a person's.

RightsPolicy.description:
What an export claims about itself.

`Commercial` is the default, because the failure this guards against is
silent and the correction is one field. An export that wants CubiCasa5K in
it has to say `research` and will say so in its manifest forever.

Role.description:
What a caller is allowed to do.

Three, not one per route. The distinction that matters is not which
endpoint but which *kind* of thing an endpoint does: read what happened,
author something that outlives the log, or ask another system to run work.

oneOf.description: Registered, or would have been under `dry_run`.

Refused, with the reason. One row's problem never fails the batch: an
import of six hundred where four have a bad URI should register five
hundred and ninety-six and say which four.

RowsBody.description: Rows, on their way to or from a worker.

RunAction.description:
Something a caller may do to a **run**, given where it got to.

The sibling of [`ContextAction`] and deliberately a separate enum: these are
done to an execution and those to a block, and one list holding both would
be a step's panel offering to stop the whole run.

It exists so a caller never re-derives a precondition. The rules are three
lines and a panel could hold them — and then there would be two copies of
`decide`'s mind, in two languages, and the day they disagree is the day
somebody trusts the wrong one. Same reasoning as `ContextAction::allowed`
and as the annotation canvas implementing no validation.

RunBlocks.description:
Which authored blocks a run's steps cover, and what they were authored as.

Every field comes from the **pinned plan**. `definition_revision` is what
makes the rest safe to draw with: a canvas holding a different revision is
holding different blocks, and lighting them from these step ids would be
borrowing one run's outcome for another run's drawing.

definition_revision.description:
The authored revision this run compiled from. Compare it with the one
the canvas was loaded at; unequal means drift, and drift means the
states below belong to blocks that are not the ones on screen.

plan_id.description:
The compiled plan, addressed over the executable fields only. Two
revisions that differ by a dragged block share this.

RunDetail.description: A run plus what is needed to draw it.

spans.description:
Spans finished so far, in completion order. A running run has fewer
spans than it eventually will — that is the point of a live view.

next_cursor.description: Pass as `before` to fetch the next page. Absent on the last page.

RunProjection.description:
The run projection a store keeps beside the stream.

Rebuildable from the stream, and updated in the same transaction that
appends to it. It exists to *accept the next command* without folding a
whole history, and for the run's own page — never as the source of a list the
event log's own folds already serve (ADR_0026).

**When a run started and ended is not here**, and that is the same rule
rather than an omission: ADR_0026 puts every managed run's facts on the log
under this id, and the workflow fold answers it with `started_at`,
`ended_at` *and* `duration_ms`. The two fields were here once, written by
nothing and read by nothing, which is the shape 43.15 is about (43.33).

payloads.description:
Where this run's words live. Shown rather than assumed: whether a
deployment is holding somebody's turns is the kind of thing that should
be readable off the run rather than inferred from a variable nobody
looking at the panel can see.

RunState.description: A stable type, and the word a person reads.

name.description: Empty means "call it by its type".

RunSummary.description: One row in the runs table.

last_checkpoint.description:
The newest checkpoint folded into this row. A client can resume the
live stream from here without re-reading the run.

last_event_at.description:
The newest event folded into this row, ended or not.

The one number that separates a run still working from a run whose
producer stopped talking. Nothing here promotes the second case to a
status — a projector that decided a run had died would be guessing
about a process it cannot see, and the guess would be wrong for every
agent that legitimately thinks for an hour. It reports when the run was
last heard from and lets the reader draw the line.

runtimes.description:
Every producing service seen on this run, in first-seen order.

A run is normally one process, but a handoff between two services keeps
the same `run_id`, and that is exactly the case worth being able to see.

workflow.description: The orchestration this run executes, when the producer names one.

RunView.description:
A run, with what may be done to it.

The actions are computed here rather than left to the caller, for
`ContextAction::allowed`'s reason one level up: a panel that decided for
itself which of cancel, pause and resume apply would be a second copy of
`decide`'s preconditions, in another language, drifting from the first.

**Compatibility.** `GET /api/v1/executions/{execution_id}` and every
command route answered with a bare `RunProjection` before this type
existed; they now answer with this. The projection is unchanged and moved
under `execution`, so a field read as `state` is read as
`execution.state`. Clients generated from `contracts/openapi.json` follow
it by regenerating; a hand-written one does not, and this is the note that
says so.

allowed.description:
Which run-level commands would be accepted right now. Empty for a run
that has finished.

Runtime.description:
Which loader reads this, and therefore what it is allowed to do.

Deliberately small, and deliberately ordered by how much of somebody else's
code runs when the artifact is opened. The first two are data formats with
a fixed interpreter; the third is a program.

allOf.description:
One Flow PHP query. Its `blocks` is what makes three boxes on the canvas
light up together: Flow executes one pipeline, so a source and its
transforms compile to one step.

oneOf.description:
One Flow PHP query. Its `blocks` is what makes three boxes on the canvas
light up together: Flow executes one pipeline, so a source and its
transforms compile to one step.

allOf.description: One marimo notebook over the rows the step before it produced.

oneOf.description: One marimo notebook over the rows the step before it produced.

allOf.description:
A dataset version, written by the serve role. The one binding that runs
in that process, and it executes nothing: it writes a
content-addressed version.

oneOf.description:
A dataset version, written by the serve role. The one binding that runs
in that process, and it executes nothing: it writes a
content-addressed version.

allOf.description: A registered function a worker pulls and runs.

oneOf.description: A registered function a worker pulls and runs.

allOf.description: Nobody runs it. It waits for somebody to answer.

oneOf.description: Nobody runs it. It waits for somebody to answer.

allOf.description:
Handed whole to an external engine through `core::engine::WorkflowEngine`.
That engine owns its internal retries; this one records the reference.

oneOf.description:
Handed whole to an external engine through `core::engine::WorkflowEngine`.
That engine owns its internal retries; this one records the reference.

RuntimeBinding.description:
Where a step runs, and everything that runtime needs.

Where each runtime executes, who owns its retries, and what it may carry.
Every variant names a *binding* and its parameters and never a host — an
executor's address is configuration, for ADR_0012's and ADR_0016's reason,
unchanged. A plan naming its own endpoint would be a request-forgery
primitive posted by anything that can reach the API.

RuntimeKind.description: The word a reactor routes on, without loading the plan.

SampleRecord.description: A point on a finer series — a learning rate, a gradient norm.

SaveProjectRequest.description: What a caller sends to create or re-describe a project.

SaveRevisionRequest.description: What a caller sends to save a drawing.

accept.description:
Promote this revision in the same call. Requires that it validates
clean, which is the only place review and validation meet.

created.description: False when this exact immutable revision was already present.
False when this exact immutable revision was already present.

SavedRevision.description: The result of saving a drawing.

created.description: False when this exact set of shapes was already stored.

Schedule.description:
A definition's schedule, as somebody set it.

**Mutable, and deliberately not part of the definition's content address.**
Changing the hour must not mint a new pipeline revision: that would be a
revision history about scheduling, which is the same mistake as making
`produced_by` part of a dataset version's identity. It lives as a head
beside the definition, the way a prompt's labels live beside its versions.

cadence.description:
A field rather than a flattened one, and not for taste: serde's
`deny_unknown_fields` and `flatten` do not compose, and the bodies here
deny unknown fields so a `cron` somebody hoped would work is named
rather than ignored. Nesting is what keeps that guardrail.

enabled.description:
Off keeps the schedule and starts nothing. Deleting it and re-typing it
next month is how a schedule gets re-typed wrongly.

timezone.description:
An IANA name — `Europe/Warsaw`, not an offset.

An offset is unambiguous and wrong twice a year: somebody who asked for
nine in the morning means nine in the morning in March and in October.
Storing the zone is what lets the answer change when the zone's rules
say it should.

ScheduleTimerBody.description: A deferred append, as a caller asks for one.

message.description:
What to append when it comes due. Composed by the caller, because an
engine that assembled one would be deciding what a timeout means.

timer_id.description: The worker's own id, unique inside this execution.

ScheduleView.description: A schedule, when it next fires, and what setting it started.

firings.description:
What the tick did, newest first.

Read from the **workflow store**, not from the schedule object. They
used to be one thing, which is what let a tick's write-back undo an
edit or resurrect a deleted schedule; configuration and slot
outcomes now have different writers and live in different places.

Empty when this deployment wired no execution store — there is then no
tick either, so nothing has fired and an empty list is the true answer
rather than a missing one.

next_run.description:
When the tick would next start it. `None` while it is off.

Answered here rather than left to the caller, and that is the same rule
as `RunView::allowed`: the panel computing it would be a second
implementation of `slots_between` — in another language, with its own
idea of when the clocks change — free to show an hour the run does not
happen at.

started.description: The run `run_now` started, when it was asked for.

effective_from.description:
When the *current cadence* began to apply.

Without it every schedule is handed the whole interval a checkpoint has
accumulated, so one written while the worker was down for
three days ran three days of slots the moment it came back — and
changing an hour during an outage re-ran the past under the new rule.

Not `updated_at`, and that is the review's own warning: an edit that
does not change *when* it fires would then quietly drop a slot that was
already due. It moves only when [`Schedule::fires_the_same_as`] says the
rule changed — which makes re-enabling an activation too, so a schedule
switched back on starts from now rather than running the days it was
off.

Optional so a schedule stored before this field existed still reads;
[`Self::effective_from`] answers for it, and the fallback is
`updated_at` because that is when such a schedule was last written.

set_by.description:
Who set it, from the session. Recorded because a run nobody remembers
asking for at three in the morning is a question with an answer.

Score.description: One metric, on the baseline and on the candidate.

Sdk.description:
Which SDK produced an event.

Serialised as a plain string with an unknown value passing through: an SDK
this backend has never heard of must still be able to publish.

SetScheduleBody.description:
What a caller sets.

`deny_unknown_fields`, like every other command body here: a `cron` somebody
hoped would work is a 400 naming it rather than a field that is ignored and
reads as accepted.

request_id.description:
What makes two `run_now` requests the same request.

The execution id is derived from it, so a retry — a proxy repeating the
PUT, a click on a button whose first response was slow — lands on the
run it already started instead of beside it. Without it the id comes
from the second the request arrived in, which made a retry one second
later a second run.

Any stable string the caller minds: the panel sends one per user
action.

run_now.description: Start it once, now, as well as saving it.

timezone.description: An IANA name — `Europe/Warsaw`. Never an offset; see [`Schedule`].

Settled.description: What the decider did with a report.

ShardRef.description:
One written shard of a staged artifact.

The unit of resume and the unit of proof. `digest` is over the shard's
plaintext bytes — before any encryption, so an archive that seals its
shards and an importer that does not produce comparable references — and it
is what [`version_of`] builds the artifact's identity from.

digest.description:
`sha256` of the shard's plaintext JSONL. What proves a shard was not
swapped for another.

SlotKey.description:
The slot a definition is due for, as a key.

The slot is the *intended* instant and never the moment the tick noticed
it: a run started late after an outage belongs to the nine o'clock it was
for, which is also what makes the derived execution id stable across a
replay.

SlotOutcome.description:
What the tick decided about one slot. Terminal: a settled slot is done.

**The scheduler's own decision, and never the run's outcome.** Whether the
run then succeeded is on the event log, which the Workflows view folds, and
a second copy here would be free to disagree with it (ADR_0026).

The three the previous release's `FiringOutcome` had, unchanged, because
the panel already renders them and they are already what a person reads.

detail.description:
Why it was refused — or, while it is unsettled, what the last attempt
ran into. A slot that has been failing every tick says what is wrong
with it rather than looking untouched.

execution_id.description: The run this slot started, or the one that blocked it.

lease_owner.description: Who is trying, and since when. Absent once it is settled.

oneOf.description: `None` while it is still being decided.

SlotRecord.description:
A slot as the store holds it.

Flat rather than an outcome carrying its own fields, and that is not
laziness: it is one row in `schedule_slots` and one shape the panel already
renders, so a column, a field and a rendered line are the same three things
end to end.

Source.description: Who sent the event. Enough to find the process that produced a bad batch.

SourceCatalog.description:
A loaded catalogue: the corpora somebody checked, and where to look for more.

Cloneable and cheap to hold. An instance loads one at start-up and every
reader shares it — the alternative, re-reading a file per request, would
make the answer depend on when it was asked.

SourceDirectory.description: A place to go looking, rather than a corpus.

SourceFile.description: One file a batch was read out of, as the hub described it.

digest.description:
Whatever the hub published: an LFS `sha256`, a git blob id, an ETag.
Never verified here, because these bytes are not the bytes this
registry stores — an image is hashed on arrival and *that* digest is
its identity.

total.description:
Rows before the filter, so a caller can tell an empty filter from an
empty table.

SourceUsage.description: What the licence permits, stated conservatively.

total_known.description: Spans matching the filter, before the page limit.

SpanRow.description: One span, flattened for a list rather than for a tree.

operation.description:
The four attributes worth filtering on, lifted out of `attributes` so
the panel does not have to walk the list to render a row.

run_id.description: From the map key: a `CompletedSpan` carries no run id of its own.

Split.description: Which side of the split a family is on.

SplitRatios.description: How families are dealt out. Percentages, summing to 100.

StageBatchRequest.description:
What a batch is for, decided once and pinned.

Rights, evidence and source sit here rather than on each page because they
are properties of the *corpus*: a per-page field would invite a pipeline to
derive them from a column, which is the mirror's word laundered through a
`withEntry`. This is also the "pinned source" half of "re-running the same
pinned source and pipeline yields the same version".

evidence.description: Who checked that, where and when. Recorded, never enforced.

rights.description: What the caller asserts may be done with every image in this batch.

StagedBatch.description: A batch as it sits in the store.

digest.description: `sha256(request ‖ every page digest, in order)`, once sealed.

pages.description:
One entry per stored page, in order. The same [`ShardRef`] the
conversation export writes, because it is the same thing: an ordered,
digested piece of a staged artifact.

request_digest.description: What was asked for, hashed. Half of the batch's content address.

sealed.description: True once the batch takes no more rows. Set by queueing a job.

singleton_pages.description:
Pages on which no two rows shared a `group_id`.

The family split is the one mistake an import cannot detect afterwards:
a `group_id` mapped from the file name gives every image its own
family, the test score then measures memorisation, and nothing in the
numbers says so. Counted per page rather than over the whole batch
because the alternative is a set of every group id a million-row import
has seen, held in a manifest — so what this supports is the exact
statement "every page of this batch gave each row its own family",
which is what a filename mapping produces and what a real one does not.

StartExecutionBody.description:
What a caller may ask this system to run.

Note what is not here, which is the same absence as `LaunchBody`'s and
`RerunBody`'s: no endpoint, no script, no host. A plan names a binding and
its parameters, and every executor's address is configuration.
`deny_unknown_fields` so an attempt to supply one — or a `backend`, a `mode`
or a `publish` flag that is not implemented — is a 400 naming it rather than
a field silently ignored that reads as accepted.

as_of.description:
Where that window ends, in seconds since the epoch. `None` is now.

Two runs that pin the same span compile to one `plan_id` and one cache
key, which is what makes a scheduled build of a fixed period cheap the
second time. Left out, every run pins a fresh span — which is right for
"curate the last hour" and is why a hit is something a caller asks for
rather than something they get by accident.

decided_by.description:
Who decides what runs next. Left out, this system does — which is what
every curation pipeline and every scheduled run wants, and what this
route did before the field existed.

parameters.description: Values bound when the execution was requested, available to every step.

oneOf.description:
Where this run's words live. Left out, the deployment's default, which
is `external` unless somebody set otherwise: the content stays with the
worker and this instance holds a reference, a digest and a size.

`sealed` sends the content here to be encrypted under the conversation
archive's keys, and is refused — naming both variables — when this
instance has no archive. It is never quietly downgraded: a run that
asked for its words to be sealed and got them kept somewhere else
instead is the failure the whole policy exists to prevent.

window_seconds.description:
How wide the source's time window is, in seconds.

Resolved to exact bounds **here**, once, rather than at dispatch: the
plan then records what it was asked for, a retry reads the same rows,
and a cache key can exist at all.

StateType.description: What drives orchestration. Nine, and no more without a reason written down.

StepBlocks.description: One plan step, and the blocks somebody drew that became it.

blocks.description:
The authored block ids, in order. Empty for a step no canvas block
compiled to, where the step id is the address.

StepBreakdown.description:
Retrieval, embedding, rerank, guardrail — grouped by kind, then by name.

Retrieval latency is the number a slow RAG turn gets debugged against, and
it is invisible in the LLM and tool breakdowns.

StepState.description: The logical state of one plan step, across every attempt it took.

current_attempt.description: The attempt number in flight, or the last one taken. `0` before any.

StoredBlob.description: A stored image blob and what it is.

created.description: False when these exact bytes were already stored.

image_id.description: SHA-256 of the bytes, computed here. This is the `image_id`.

StreamAppended.description: Where the stream got to, and whether this call is what put it there.

created.description:
`false` when this batch had already been appended — a redelivery, not a
race. The worker carries on from `version` either way.

version.description: The version to send as the next `expected_version`.

StreamName.description:
The stream a run's events live on.

One stream per **run**, not per conversation: a conversation can fan out
into several agent runs at once, and partitioning the log by conversation
would serialise runs that have no reason to wait for each other.

SuiteSummary.description:
A suite on a dataset, across every evaluation of it that is retained.

The level above a report, and the one MLflow calls an experiment.

latest_metrics.description:
The newest finished evaluation's metrics, and the change from the one
before it. A number with no direction is the thing an evaluation page
is usually accused of being.

TargetKind.description:
What kind of definition is being run.

Two arms, which is what the enum was for: both compile to the same
`ExecutionPlan` from different editors, with different provenance, and the
names live in different registries under different prefixes. A
`kind` nobody had to send would have to be guessed from the name — and two
definitions may share one, which is exactly what `WorkflowSpec` being saved
beside `CurationPipeline` allows.

TensorSpec.description:
A number a request has to look like.

The shape is a list rather than a string so a server can check it; `None`
in a dimension is "any", which is how a batch axis is written. A runtime
that validates against this refuses a wrong request instead of reshaping it
into something that predicts confidently and wrongly.

classes.description:
For a classifier: what index 0, 1, 2 … mean.

On the package rather than in the serving code, because a label order
that lives in a deployment is a label order that silently permutes when
somebody retrains — every metric stays finite and nothing says so. The
same failure `ExportDataset` checks `schema_version` for.

dtype.description:
`float32`, `int64`, `uint8`. Free text, because the vocabulary is the
runtime's and an enum here would be one framework's list imposed on
every other.

Timer.description:
A message a hosted decider asked this engine to append later.

The one *active* thing this engine does for a hosted run, and it is
deliberately the smallest possible active thing: a deferred append.
The worker composes the message when it schedules the timer, and the engine
stores it and hands it back at the time — so "the engine does not interpret
the messages" survives intact. It is not reading a stream to work out that
something is due; it was told, explicitly, in a row.

## Why a row rather than the stream

`agentic.workflow.Saga` already keeps its timers *in* the stream, as
`saga.timeout_scheduled` events, and works out what is due by folding it.
That fold is the worker's and stays the worker's. What it cannot do from
there is *notice*: nothing wakes up and looks. A row is what an index over
every hosted run can be built on, so one tick finds what is due across all
of them without reading a single stream.

message.description:
What to append when it comes due. Composed by the worker at the moment
it schedules, never assembled here — an engine that built this would be
deciding what a timeout means.

timer_id.description:
The worker's own id, unique inside one execution. `agentic`'s
`timeout_id`, and the reason a repeated schedule is one timer.

oneOf.description:
Hold this message until `due_at`. Scheduling one id twice is one timer,
which is what makes a decider's retry safe.

schedule.description:
Hold this message until `due_at`. Scheduling one id twice is one timer,
which is what makes a decider's retry safe.

oneOf.description:
Withdraw it. A no-op when there is none, because a saga that cancels a
timeout it already handled is doing the ordinary thing.

cancel.description:
Withdraw it. A no-op when there is none, because a saga that cancels a
timeout it already handled is doing the ordinary thing.

TimerBody.description:
One thing to do to this execution's timers.

A tagged pair rather than a struct with a `cancel` flag, because the two
carry different fields and a body that could name a `due_at` while
cancelling would be a shape with a meaningless half.

ToolResult.description:
What a tool handed back.

Attached to the turn rather than folded into a `Text` part, because a
failure is a training signal and a stringified error is not: an SFT shape
wants the successful ones, a preference shape often wants exactly the pairs
where one branch failed.

cache_hit_ratio.description:
Cached as a share of input. The one number that says whether prompt
caching is doing anything.

step_calls.description:
Retrievals, embeddings, reranks, guardrails — everything traced as a
step rather than as an LLM or tool call.

TrainingRun.description: One training run, with everything it accumulated.

code.description: The code that ran. A git revision, usually.

dataset.description:
`project@export-sha256` from the annotation registry. A bare project
name is recorded and marks the run irreproducible rather than being
refused: a smoke test on an unversioned dataset is a legitimate thing
to do, and refusing it would only teach people to lie about it.

last_heard_from.description:
When this run last wrote anything. The only honest answer to "is it
still alive", and the field a reader draws a stall from.

model.description:
The model being trained — a name, not a version. The version is what
this run *produces*; see [`crate::model::ModelVersion`].

reproducible.description:
Whether this run can be pointed at afterwards and repeated. Decided
once, when the run opens, and stored rather than re-derived: a rule
computed in three places is a rule three places can disagree about, and
the panel is one of them.

sample_decimations.description:
How many times the sampled series has been halved. The effective
interval is the original one times two to this power, and saying so is
what stops somebody reading a decimated curve as a complete one.

workflow_run_id.description:
Set when the orchestrator launched this run, so it joins the workflow
execution it belongs to. See ADR_0012 and ADR_0016.

TrainingRunSummary.description: A run as it appears in a list: everything but the curve.

TrainingScope.description:
What the consent covers.

Separate scopes rather than one "may train" flag, because they are
genuinely different permissions and the difference is where the accidents
happen: an evaluation set that quietly becomes a training set is the same
mistake as a research-licensed corpus in a commercial model, one field over.

TrainingStatus.description:
Where a run is.

`Running` is the *absence* of an end, not a claim that anything is
happening — exactly the rule the projector follows for agent runs. A
trainer killed by an OOM and a trainer thinking for twenty minutes look
identical from here, so nothing in this crate decides which one it is.
[`TrainingRun::last_heard_from`] is what a reader draws the line from.

TurnContent.description:
The half that is encrypted.

A type of its own rather than two fields on the head, because the split is
the security boundary: everything in here is sealed, everything outside it
is readable by anyone who may list the archive, and a field that moved
across the line by accident would be a leak nobody could see in a diff.

next_offset.description: Where to resume. Absent at the end of the conversation.

oneOf.description:
Which of two answers was better, where a reviewer said.

A different axis from [`Self::state`], and keeping them separate is the
point. `state` answers "may this content be used at all" — the safety
gate. This answers "was it a good answer" — the quality one. A
preference pair is built from two turns that both passed the first and
disagree on the second, which is what stops a turn rejected for holding
somebody's address becoming the rejected half of a preference pair and
putting that address in the corpus anyway.

TurnReviewRequest.description: One reviewer's decision about one turn.

findings.description:
What the reviewer saw that the scanner did not — an unsafe answer, a
name the rules do not recognise. Appended to the turn's findings rather
than replacing them: a scanner finding a human disagreed with is a fact
about both of them.

oneOf.description:
The quality judgement, where the reviewer is making one. Only a turn
this is set on can take part in a preference export, and nothing infers
it — a rejection has many reasons and only one of them is "the other
answer was better".

TurnReviewState.description: Whether a human has decided about this turn.

TurnState.description: Whether the content is still there.

oneOf.description:
Produced here, or supplied with an explicit grant covering training,
derived artifacts and the resulting weights.
Licensed under terms that permit commercial use.
Licensed for research only — CC BY-NC and everything shaped like it.

Nobody has checked. Usable for an experiment, excluded from anything
that claims a policy.

UsageRights.description: What may be done with an image, and therefore with a model trained on it.

oneOf.description: A person wrote it, or it was imported from a repository.

An optimiser produced it. `optimization_id` is the record that says
what it was measured against.

VersionOrigin.description:
Where a version came from.

The distinction the panel needs to answer "did a person write this, or did
an optimiser?" — which is the first question asked about a prompt that is
behaving strangely.

Withdrawal.description:
